newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: FOCUS-Little effect seen from Czech cen bank move.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Little effect seen from Czech cen bank move.

text.p: The Czech National Bank's (CNB) largest step in weeks to ease its grip on the crown should have little effect on the currency or the market in general, analysts said on Thursday.

The CNB said that from Friday, it would re-open banks' access to its last resort Lombard lending facility at a rate of 50 percent. The facility was closed in late May after the currency came under pressure from a wave of speculative selling.

Analysts said that while the move was a positive sign, it would have little effect on the crown since it was not coupled with an easing of unofficial restrictions on non-resident access to the local money market.

"We see from the rate that the central bank is being very careful, but it is important to note that foreigners still do not have global access to the crown," said Petr Benes of Nomura International in London.

Downward pressure on the crown forced the CNB to adopt measures to defend the currency in May, including choking market liquidity by cutting access to the Lombard facility and reaching an informal agreement with large local banks to cut access to the Czech money market by non-residents.
During the crown crisis, the CNB also intervened directly on the market and raised its discount rate to 13 percent from a previous 10.5 percent and the Lombard rate to 50 percent from 14 percent.

"There is still the restriction for non-residents, so we will probably have to wait for the cutting of one of the key interest rates. It's a first step but not so important for the market," said Tomas Becvar a forex dealer at Komerncni Banka.
In announcing the move, CNB spokesman Martin Svehla told Reuters the central bank is planning to remove money market restrictions at the appropriate time.
"We have the intention, for sure (to remove the informal limits on non-residents), but I cannot specify now when and how we will do this."

The CNB had been loosening its grip on market liquidity in recent days, mainly through its repo rate, which has fallen from 75 percent to 31 percent. Before the crown crisis, the central bank repo rate stood at 12.9 percent.
Svehla indicated that more moves would be taken, but only once circumstances allow. "As we move toward a more standard situation we will go gradually down with interest rates," he said.

The crown showed little immediate reaction to the move, trading at about 18.691 against the mark and 32.181 against the dollar in late Thursday activity. Just before the announcement, the crown was at 32.186 to the dollar and 18.689 to the mark.
Dealers said the crown should continue trading in a narrow range between 18.5 and 19.0 against the mark in the coming days.
But some warned the central bank still needed to make several more moves on interest rates and that this might prompt investors to go on the offensive and once again push the crown lower.
"They (the CNB) cannot keep rates so high for such a long time. And they cannot keep foreigners behind the door for much longer," said one Frankfurt-based trader.

"At this moment there is still the Czech crown environment which is very good for short-selling. Whenever the CNB goes down with rates, it will be watched very carefully with speculators...and there could be another attack on the crown."
